fetched_contents.text: Early Goal-Directed Therapy in the Treatment of Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock Abstract Background Goal-directed therapy has been used for severe sepsis and septic shock in the intensive care unit. This approach involves adjustments of cardiac preload, afterload, and contractility to balance oxygen delivery with oxygen demand. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of early goal-directed therapy before admission to the intensive care unit. Methods We randomly assigned patients who arrived at an urban emergency department with severe sepsis or septic shock to receive either six hours of early goal-directed therapy or standard therapy (as a control) before admission to the intensive care unit. Clinicians who subsequently assumed the care of the patients were blinded to the treatment assignment. In-hospital mortality (the primary efficacy outcome), end points with respect to resuscitation, and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II) scores were obtained serially for 72 hours and compared between the study groups. Results Of the 263 enrolled patients, 130 were randomly assigned to early goal-directed therapy and 133 to standard therapy; there were no significant differences between the groups with respect to base-line characteristics. In-hospital mortality was 30.5 percent in the group assigned to early goal-directed therapy, as compared with 46.5 percent in the group assigned to standard therapy (P=0.009). During the interval from 7 to 72 hours, the patients assigned to early goal-directed therapy had a significantly higher mean (±SD) central venous oxygen saturation (70.4±10.7 percent vs. 65.3±11.4 percent), a lower lactate concentration (3.0±4.4 vs. 3.9±4.4 mmol per liter), a lower base deficit (2.0±6.6 vs. 5.1±6.7 mmol per liter), and a higher pH (7.40±0.12 vs. 7.36±0.12) than the patients assigned to standard therapy (P≤0.02 for all comparisons). During the same period, mean APACHE II scores were significantly lower, indicating less severe organ dysfunction, in the patients assigned to early goal-directed therapy than in those assigned to standard therapy (13.0±6.3 vs. 15.9±6.4, P<0.001). Conclusions Early goal-directed therapy provides significant benefits with respect to outcome in patients with severe sepsis and septic shock. The systemic inflammatory response syndrome can be self-limited or can progress to severe sepsis and septic shock.1 Along this continuum, circulatory abnormalities (intravascular volume depletion, peripheral vasodilatation, myocardial depression, and increased metabolism) lead to an imbalance between systemic oxygen delivery and oxygen demand, resulting in global tissue hypoxia or shock.2 An indicator of serious illness, global tissue hypoxia is a key development preceding multiorgan failure and death.2 The transition to serious illness occurs during the critical “golden hours,” when definitive recognition and treatment provide maximal benefit in terms of outcome. These golden hours may elapse in the emergency department,3 hospital ward,4 or the intensive care unit.5 Early hemodynamic assessment on the basis of physical findings, vital signs, central venous pressure,6 and urinary output7 fails to detect persistent global tissue hypoxia. A more definitive resuscitation strategy involves goal-oriented manipulation of cardiac preload, afterload, and contractility to achieve a balance between systemic oxygen delivery and oxygen demand.2 End points used to confirm the achievement of such a balance (hereafter called resuscitation end points) include normalized values for mixed venous oxygen saturation, arterial lactate concentration, base deficit, and pH.8 Mixed venous oxygen saturation has been shown to be a surrogate for the cardiac index as a target for hemodynamic therapy.9 In cases in which the insertion of a pulmonary-artery catheter is impractical, venous oxygen saturation can be measured in the central circulation.10 Whereas the incidence of septic shock has steadily increased during the past several decades, the associated mortality rates have remained constant or have decreased only slightly.11 Studies of interventions such as immunotherapy,12 hemodynamic optimization,9,13 or pulmonary-artery catheterization14 enrolled patients up to 72 hours after admission to the intensive care unit. The negative results of studies of the use of hemodynamic variables as end points (“hemodynamic optimization”), in particular, prompted suggestions that future studies involve patients with similar causes of disease13 or with global tissue hypoxia (as reflected by elevated lactate concentrations)15 and that they examine interventions begun at an earlier stage of disease.16,17 We examined whether early goal-directed therapy before admission to the intensive care unit effectively reduces the incidence of multiorgan dysfunction, mortality, and the use of health care resources among patients with severe sepsis or septic shock. fetched_contents.text: A systematic review and meta-analysis of early goal-directed therapy for septic shock: the ARISE, ProCESS and ProMISe Investigators Purpose: To determine whether early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) reduces mortality compared with other resuscitation strategies for patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with septic shock. Methods: Using a search strategy of PubMed, EmBase and CENTRAL, we selected all relevant randomised clinical trials published from January 2000 to January 2015. We translated non-English papers and contacted authors as necessary. Our primary analysis generated a pooled odds ratio (OR) from a fixed-effect model. Sensitivity analyses explored the effect of including non-ED studies, adjusting for study quality, and conducting a random-effects model. Secondary outcomes included organ support and hospital and ICU length of stay. Results: From 2395 initially eligible abstracts, five randomised clinical trials (n = 4735 patients) met all criteria and generally scored high for quality except for lack of blinding. There was no effect on the primary mortality outcome (EGDT: 23.2% [495/2134] versus control: 22.4% [582/2601]; pooled OR 1.01 [95% CI 0.88-1.16], P = 0.9, with heterogeneity [I(2) = 57%; P = 0.055]). The pooled estimate of 90-day mortality from the three recent multicentre studies (n = 4063) also showed no difference [pooled OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.86-1.15), P = 0.93] with no heterogeneity (I(2) = 0.0%; P = 0.97). EGDT increased vasopressor use (OR 1.25 [95% CI 1.10-1.41]; P < 0.001) and ICU admission [OR 2.19 (95% CI 1.82-2.65); P < 0.001]. Including six non-ED randomised trials increased heterogeneity (I(2) = 71%; P < 0.001) but did not change overall results [pooled OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.07); P = 0.33]. Conclusion: EGDT is not superior to usual care for ED patients with septic shock but is associated with increased utilisation of ICU resources.

fetched_contents.text: Heterogeneity in the Effect of Early Goal-Directed Therapy for Septic Shock: A Secondary Analysis of Two Multicenter International Trials . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2026 Jan 1. Abstract Objective: The optimal approach for resuscitation in septic shock remains unclear despite multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Our objective was to investigate whether previously uncharacterized variation across individuals in their response to resuscitation strategies may contribute to conflicting average treatment effects in prior RCTs. Design: We randomly split study sites from the ARISE and ProCESS trials into derivation and validation cohorts. We trained machine learning models to predict individual absolute risk differences (iARDs) in 90-day mortality and tested for heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) in derivation and validation cohorts and swapped these cohorts in sensitivity analyses. We fit the best-performing model in a combined dataset to explore roles of patient characteristics and individual components of EGDT to determine treatment responses. Setting: 81 sites in Australia, New Zealand, Hong Kong, Finland, Republic of Ireland, and the United States Patients: Adult patients presenting to the emergency room with severe sepsis or septic shock. Interventions: Early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) versus usual care. Measurements and Main Results: A local-linear random forest model performed best in predicting iARDs. In the validation cohort, HTE was confirmed, evidenced by an interaction between iARD prediction and treatment (p<0.001). When patients were grouped based on predicted iARDs, treatment response increased from the lowest to the highest quintiles (absolute risk difference [95% CI] -8% [-19%, 4%] and relative risk reduction 1.34 [0.89, 2.01] in quintile 1 suggesting harm from EGDT, and 12% [1%, 23%] and 0.64 [0.42, 0.96] in quintile 5 suggesting benefit). Sensitivity analyses showed similar findings. Pre-intervention albumin contributed the most to HTE. Analyses of individual EGDT components were inconclusive. Conclusions: Treatment response to EGDT varied across patients 86 in two multicenter RCTs with large benefits for some patients while others were harmed. Patient characteristics, including albumin, were most important in identifying HTE. Keywords: precision medicine, sepsis, machine learning, heterogeneity of treatment effect, resuscitation ---------------------------------------- Over 50 randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have tested resuscitation strategies in sepsis,(1) but the optimal approach remains uncertain. Early goal-directed therapy (EGDT), a multicomponent, six-hour intervention consisting of protocolized administration of fluids, vasopressors, inotropes, and blood products, demonstrated an absolute mortality risk reduction of 16% compared with usual care in a landmark single-center trial.(2) However, three subsequent multicenter, international RCTs (3–5) did not reproduce the previously observed benefits. Currently, the EGDT protocol is not followed routinely in clinical practice, but several components, such as the volume and rate of fluid administration and vasopressor use, remain the cornerstone of resuscitation. Importantly, the optimal way each of these components is delivered remains a source of ongoing debate and inquiry.(6–8) There has been increasing awareness that the average treatment effect (ATE) estimated in an RCT may not reflect the varying individual treatment effect experienced by each patient.(9–11) Although an individual patient data meta-analysis (IPDMA) of prior EGDT trials using conventional statistical approaches, which may have been underpowered, did not uncover subgroups that benefitted (12), heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) may exist and contribute to inconsistent results. Mini-report on what the enrolled studies found about mortality

The enrolled studies show mixed but generally modest findings: some trials reported benefit, others no difference, and one meta-analysis found no overall advantage of EGDT over usual care. In the landmark EGDT trial, in-hospital mortality was 30.5% in the EGDT group versus 46.5% in the usual-care group, which is a notable benefit of about 16 percentage points [N1-F1]. However, subsequent trials and meta-analyses did not consistently replicate this benefit. A meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock found no difference in primary mortality (pooled OR 1.01; 95% CI 0.88–1.16) and no difference in 90-day mortality from three multicenter studies (pooled OR 0.99; 95% CI 0.86–1.15) [N3-F2]. Another meta-analysis similarly found that EGDT was not superior to usual care for ED patients with septic shock, and a separate meta-analysis reported a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.67–1.08) for mortality, with heterogeneity [N3-R5].

Study populations matter a lot. The landmark trial included adult patients with severe sepsis or septic shock presenting to an emergency department, with baseline characteristics balanced between groups [N1-F1]. In contrast, the meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock included five RCTs (n=4735), while the broader meta-analysis of early EGDT included non-ED studies as well [N3-F2]. A later meta-analysis also included patients presenting to the ED with septic shock and reported no mortality benefit from EGDT [N3-R4]. The ProMISe trial, a protocolized 6-hour EGDT study, reported no reduction in 90-day mortality versus usual resuscitation, though the excerpt here is incomplete and should be treated as a summary rather than a direct quote [N2-R2]. A separate trial-level meta-analysis of individual patient data also found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3].

Outcomes span short-term and longer-term. The landmark trial reported in-hospital mortality [N1-F1]. Other studies report 28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality, with some suggesting benefit but not statistical significance [N2-R1]. The meta-analyses specifically emphasize 90-day mortality as the primary outcome [N3-F2]. A second meta-analysis also included 28-day mortality and reported EGDT decreased it, though not significantly [N2-R1]. Overall, the evidence base includes both short-term and longer-term endpoints, but the most consistent meta-analysis-level conclusion is no overall mortality advantage versus usual care [N3-F2][N3-R5].

Mini-report on why the results may differ across studies

The results differ across studies because EGDT protocols and implementation vary, patient selection and disease severity differ, and outcome measurement and follow-up differ. First, EGDT implementation is not uniform. The landmark trial used protocolized early goal-directed therapy before ICU admission, with predefined interventions and blinded care after randomization [N1-F1]. In contrast, the ProMISe trial used protocolized 6-hour EGDT versus usual resuscitation, and the later meta-analysis included non-ED studies, which may have different care settings and intervention components [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity-focused secondary analysis of two multicenter trials also emphasized that treatment response varied across patients and that the EGDT protocol is multicomponent, with fluid, vasopressors, inotropes, and blood products [N4-F3]. This suggests that implementation details matter, including whether care is strictly protocolized, how interventions are delivered, and whether blinding or standardization is preserved [N4-F3].

Second, patient selection and disease severity differ across studies. The landmark trial included adults with severe sepsis or septic shock arriving at an emergency department, with balanced baseline characteristics [N1-F1]. The broader meta-analysis included patients with septic shock and severe sepsis, while the ED-specific meta-analysis included ED patients with septic shock [N3-F2][N3-R4]. A separate heterogeneity analysis noted that the optimal resuscitation approach remains unclear despite many RCTs, and that the average treatment effect may not reflect individual responses [N4-F3]. This implies that enrollment criteria, baseline severity, and the stage of disease at presentation may influence outcomes [N4-F3].

Third, outcome measurement and follow-up differ. The landmark trial reported in-hospital mortality as the primary outcome, with serial endpoints and APACHE II scores [N1-F1]. Other studies report 28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality, with some using 90-day mortality as the primary outcome [N2-R1][N3-F2]. The meta-analysis also included secondary outcomes such as organ support and length of stay [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity analysis noted that the “dose” of intervention—amount of fluid or vasopressor—varies across patients, which complicates comparison across trials [N4-F3]. These differences in endpoints and follow-up intervals can explain why some studies show benefit, others no difference, and others show harm [N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

Mini-report on limitations and interpretation of the evidence

The evidence has important limitations, including study quality issues, risk of bias, sample size, and statistical power, and the results depend heavily on specific subgroups. First, study quality and risk of bias matter. The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock reported that the included trials generally scored high for quality except for lack of blinding [N3-F2]. The landmark trial did use blinding for clinicians after randomization, which is a strength, but the broader meta-analysis included non-ED studies and noted heterogeneity across trial designs [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity analysis also emphasized that average treatment effects in RCTs may not reflect individual treatment effects and that conventional statistical approaches may have been underpowered [N4-F3]. This suggests that bias and imprecision can limit interpretation.

Second, sample size and statistical power are relevant. The landmark trial had only 263 enrolled patients, with 130 in each group [N1-F1]. By contrast, the meta-analysis included 4735 patients across five trials and 4063 patients in three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. Larger studies can detect smaller effects, but the meta-analysis still found no mortality benefit overall and only weak heterogeneity in some models [N3-F2]. The heterogeneity analysis also noted that 50 randomized clinical trials have tested resuscitation strategies in sepsis, but the optimal approach remains uncertain, highlighting the difficulty of reconciling inconsistent results across many studies [N4-F3].

Third, the results depend on specific subgroups. The heterogeneity analysis found individual treatment effects varied across patients, with some harmed by EGDT and others benefiting, and albumin contributed most to heterogeneity [N4-F3]. The meta-analysis of individual patient data similarly found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3]. The broader meta-analysis also reported heterogeneity in pooled estimates and noted that including non-ED trials increased heterogeneity [N3-F2]. This means the evidence is not uniformly supportive of EGDT; the benefit, if any, may be concentrated in specific subgroups rather than a general population effect [N4-F3][N3-F2].

Mini-report on trial-level heterogeneity and subgroup differences

Trial-level heterogeneity and subgroup differences are central to interpreting the EGDT evidence. At the trial level, the meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock found no overall mortality benefit and no heterogeneity in the pooled 90-day mortality estimate from three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. However, including non-ED trials increased heterogeneity [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity-focused secondary analysis of two multicenter trials found that treatment response varied across patients, with large benefits for some and harm for others [N4-F3]. In that analysis, a machine learning model predicted individual absolute risk differences, and the validation cohort showed heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE), with treatment response increasing from the lowest to highest quintiles of predicted risk difference [N4-F3]. The lowest quintile showed harm from EGDT, while the highest quintile suggested benefit [N4-F3].

Which patient or intervention factors explain inconsistent results? The heterogeneity analysis identified albumin as the most important predictor of HTE, suggesting that baseline patient characteristics play a major role in explaining why some patients benefit and others do not [N4-F3]. It also noted that EGDT is a multicomponent intervention, so differences in subcomponents may explain some of the variation, but analyses of individual EGDT components were inconclusive [N4-F3]. The broader meta-analysis similarly emphasized heterogeneity in the effect of EGDT across studies [N3-R5]. This indicates that neither a single protocol nor a single patient profile fully explains the inconsistent results.

How much heterogeneity is explained by study design or protocol? The heterogeneity analysis explicitly sought to determine whether patient characteristics or features of intervention delivery could explain HTE, and it concluded that albumin and other patient characteristics were most important, while individual EGDT components were inconclusive [N4-F3]. The meta-analysis also noted that including non-ED trials increased heterogeneity [N3-F2]. This suggests that study design and protocol are part of the reason for heterogeneity, but they are not the only driver; patient-level factors appear to be a major explanatory variable [N4-F3][N3-F2].

# Integrated final answer: How does early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) impact mortality compared to usual care?

## Short answer
The enrolled studies and meta-analyses show **mixed evidence**. A landmark trial found a clear mortality benefit, but subsequent trials and the best meta-analyses found **no overall mortality advantage** of EGDT over usual care. The results also depend heavily on study population, protocol, implementation, and subgroup characteristics. So, the simple answer is: **EGDT may help some patients, but the evidence does not consistently support a general mortality benefit** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 1) What the enrolled studies found about mortality
The enrolled studies produced a **mixed pattern** of results. In the landmark trial, EGDT reduced in-hospital mortality from 46.5% in the usual-care group to 30.5% in the EGDT group, a **16 percentage-point difference** [N1-F1]. This is the strongest direct evidence in the provided branch reports. However, later studies and meta-analyses did not replicate that benefit so clearly.

A meta-analysis of emergency-department patients with septic shock found **no mortality benefit** overall, with a pooled odds ratio of 1.01 (95% CI 0.88–1.16) and no difference in 90-day mortality from three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. Another meta-analysis also reported no superiority of EGDT for ED patients with septic shock, and a separate meta-analysis found a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.67–1.08) for mortality, with heterogeneity [N3-R5][N3-R4]. A trial-level meta-analysis of individual patient data similarly found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3]. One trial also reported no reduction in 90-day mortality versus usual resuscitation [N2-R2].

So the mortality picture is: **some trials showed benefit, some showed no difference, and the most consistent meta-analyses found no overall mortality advantage** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 2) Which study populations were included and why that matters
The study populations matter a lot because they are not all the same.

- The landmark trial included **adult patients with severe sepsis or septic shock presenting to an emergency department**, with balanced baseline characteristics [N1-F1].
- The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock included **five RCTs** totaling 4735 patients [N3-F2].
- The broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies** as well, which changed the pooled results and increased heterogeneity [N3-F2].
- Another meta-analysis focused specifically on **patients presenting to the ED with septic shock** and reported no mortality benefit from EGDT [N3-R4].

This is important because the setting, disease severity, and timing of intervention can affect outcomes. The landmark trial may have captured a more responsive patient cohort, whereas later trials may have included more heterogeneous or less severely ill patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The branch reports also emphasize that the optimal resuscitation approach remains unclear despite many RCTs, which suggests that the observed differences may reflect real biological variation rather than a single “right” protocol [N4-F3].

## 3) Short-term versus longer-term outcomes
Outcomes span **short-term and longer-term endpoints**.

- The landmark trial reported **in-hospital mortality** as the primary outcome [N1-F1].
- Other studies report **28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality**, with some suggesting benefit but not statistical significance [N2-R1].
- The meta-analyses emphasize **90-day mortality** as the primary outcome [N3-F2].

So the evidence base is not limited to one endpoint. However, the most consistent meta-analysis-level conclusion is that, for ED patients with septic shock, EGDT does **not appear to improve mortality overall** [N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 4) Why results may differ across studies
There are several reasons the results differ across studies.

### a) Differences in EGDT protocol and implementation
EGDT is not implemented in the same way across all studies. The landmark trial used **protocolized early goal-directed therapy before ICU admission**, with predefined interventions and blinded care after randomization [N1-F1]. In contrast, the ProMISe trial used **protocolized 6-hour EGDT versus usual resuscitation**, and the broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies**, which likely had different care settings and intervention components [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity-focused analysis also emphasized that EGDT is a **multicomponent intervention** involving fluids, vasopressors, inotropes, and blood products, and that treatment response varied across patients [N4-F3].

### b) Differences in patient selection and disease severity
Patient selection and baseline disease severity differ across studies. The landmark trial included adults with **severe sepsis or septic shock arriving at the ED**, while later meta-analyses included patients with **septic shock and severe sepsis** and ED patients with **septic shock** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R4]. The branch reports also note that the optimal resuscitation approach remains uncertain, and that the average treatment effect may not reflect individual responses [N4-F3]. This suggests that enrollment criteria, baseline severity, and the stage of disease at presentation can all influence outcomes.

### c) Differences in outcome measurement and follow-up
Outcome measurement and follow-up differ across studies. The landmark trial used **in-hospital mortality** as the primary outcome, while other studies report **28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The meta-analyses also included **secondary outcomes** such as organ support and length of stay [N3-F2]. The heterogeneity analysis noted that the “dose” of intervention—such as the amount of fluid or vasopressor—varies across patients, which can complicate comparisons [N4-F3].

These differences help explain why some studies show benefit, others show no difference, and others show harm [N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

## 5) Trial-level heterogeneity and subgroup differences
Trial-level heterogeneity is central to interpreting the evidence. The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock found **no overall mortality benefit** and **no heterogeneity** in the pooled 90-day mortality estimate from three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. However, including **non-ED trials** increased heterogeneity [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity-focused secondary analysis of two multicenter trials found that **treatment response varied across patients**, with large benefits for some and harm for others [N4-F3]. In that analysis, a machine-learning model predicted individual absolute risk differences, and the validation cohort showed **heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE)**, with treatment response increasing from the lowest to the highest quintiles of predicted risk difference [N4-F3].

- The lowest quintile showed **harm** from EGDT, while the highest quintile suggested **benefit** [N4-F3].
- **Albumin** contributed the most to HTE, suggesting that patient characteristics are a major explanatory factor [N4-F3].
- Individual EGDT components were inconclusive, but the analysis explicitly sought to determine whether patient characteristics or features of intervention delivery could explain HTE [N4-F3].

So the consistent message is: **the effect of EGDT is not uniform; some patients benefit, others do not, and some may be harmed** [N4-F3].

## 6) Limitations and interpretation of the evidence
The evidence has important limitations that affect interpretation.

### a) Study quality and risk of bias
The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock reported that the included trials generally scored high for quality except for **lack of blinding** [N3-F2]. The landmark trial did use blinding for clinicians after randomization, which is a strength, but the broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies**, which may introduce additional heterogeneity [N3-F2]. The heterogeneity analysis also noted that conventional statistical approaches may have been underpowered, which can reduce confidence in subgroup findings [N4-F3].

### b) Sample size and statistical power
The landmark trial had a relatively small sample size: **263 enrolled patients**, with 130 in each group [N1-F1]. By contrast, the meta-analysis included **4735 patients** across five trials and **4063 patients** in three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. Larger studies can detect smaller effects, but the meta-analyses still found no overall mortality benefit, which suggests that the effect, if any, may be small or highly dependent on subgroups [N3-F2].

### c) Dependence on specific subgroups
The results depend heavily on **specific subgroups**. The heterogeneity analysis found that **individual treatment effects varied across patients**, with some harmed and some benefiting, and that albumin was the most important predictor of HTE [N4-F3]. The meta-analysis of individual patient data also found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3]. The broader meta-analysis similarly emphasized heterogeneity in the effect of EGDT across studies [N3-R5]. This means the benefit, if any, is likely concentrated in **particular subgroups** rather than a general population effect [N4-F3][N3-F2].

## 7) Bottom line
Combining the branch reports, the evidence supports the following conclusion:

- **Yes**: there is **one strong landmark trial** suggesting a mortality benefit with EGDT [N1-F1].
- **No overall benefit**: the best meta-analyses and trial-level analyses found **no mortality advantage** of EGDT over usual care for ED patients with septic shock [N3-F2][N3-R5].
- **Mixed results are common**: some studies show benefit, some no difference, and some show harm, especially when subgroups are examined [N2-R1][N4-F3].
- **Heterogeneity matters**: patient characteristics, protocol design, and implementation differences explain why results differ across studies [N4-F3][N3-F2].
- **Interpretation is cautious**: the evidence is limited by study quality, sample size, and subgroup dependence [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## Final judgment
If the question is “does EGDT improve mortality versus usual care?” the most defensible answer, based on the provided evidence, is: **not clearly yes.** The best-supported conclusion is that **EGDT may help some patients, but the evidence does not consistently support a broad mortality benefit** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

# Integrated final answer: How does early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) impact mortality compared to usual care?

## Short answer
The enrolled studies and meta-analyses show **mixed evidence**. A landmark trial found a clear mortality benefit, but subsequent trials and the best meta-analyses found **no overall mortality advantage** of EGDT over usual care. The results also depend heavily on study population, protocol, implementation, and subgroup characteristics. So, the simple answer is: **EGDT may help some patients, but the evidence does not consistently support a general mortality benefit** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 1) What the enrolled studies found about mortality
The enrolled studies produced a **mixed pattern** of results. In the landmark trial, EGDT reduced in-hospital mortality from 46.5% in the usual-care group to 30.5% in the EGDT group, a **16 percentage-point difference** [N1-F1]. This is the strongest direct evidence in the provided branch reports. However, later studies and meta-analyses did not replicate that benefit so clearly.

A meta-analysis of emergency-department patients with septic shock found **no mortality benefit** overall, with a pooled odds ratio of 1.01 (95% CI 0.88–1.16) and no difference in 90-day mortality from three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. Another meta-analysis also reported no superiority of EGDT for ED patients with septic shock, and a separate meta-analysis found a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.67–1.08) for mortality, with heterogeneity [N3-R5][N3-R4]. A trial-level meta-analysis of individual patient data similarly found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3]. One trial also reported no reduction in 90-day mortality versus usual resuscitation [N2-R2].

So the mortality picture is: **some trials showed benefit, some showed no difference, and the most consistent meta-analyses found no overall mortality advantage** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 2) Which study populations were included and why that matters
The study populations matter a lot because they are not all the same.

- The landmark trial included **adult patients with severe sepsis or septic shock presenting to an emergency department**, with balanced baseline characteristics [N1-F1].
- The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock included **five RCTs** totaling 4735 patients [N3-F2].
- The broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies** as well, which changed the pooled results and increased heterogeneity [N3-F2].
- Another meta-analysis focused specifically on **patients presenting to the ED with septic shock** and reported no mortality benefit from EGDT [N3-R4].

This is important because the setting, disease severity, and timing of intervention can affect outcomes. The landmark trial may have captured a more responsive patient cohort, whereas later trials may have included more heterogeneous or less severely ill patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The branch reports also emphasize that the optimal resuscitation approach remains unclear despite many RCTs, which suggests that the observed differences may reflect real biological variation rather than a single “right” protocol [N4-F3].

## 3) Short-term versus longer-term outcomes
Outcomes span **short-term and longer-term endpoints**.

- The landmark trial reported **in-hospital mortality** as the primary outcome [N1-F1].
- Other studies report **28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality**, with some suggesting benefit but not statistical significance [N2-R1].
- The meta-analyses emphasize **90-day mortality** as the primary outcome [N3-F2].

So the evidence base is not limited to one endpoint. However, the most consistent meta-analysis-level conclusion is that, for ED patients with septic shock, EGDT does **not appear to improve mortality overall** [N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 4) Why results may differ across studies
There are several reasons the results differ across studies.

### a) Differences in EGDT protocol and implementation
EGDT is not implemented in the same way across all studies. The landmark trial used **protocolized early goal-directed therapy before ICU admission**, with predefined interventions and blinded care after randomization [N1-F1]. In contrast, the ProMISe trial used **protocolized 6-hour EGDT versus usual resuscitation**, and the broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies**, which likely had different care settings and intervention components [N3-F2]. # Integrated final answer: How does early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) impact mortality compared to usual care?

## Short answer
The enrolled studies and meta-analyses show **mixed evidence**. A landmark trial found a clear mortality benefit, but subsequent trials and the best meta-analyses found **no overall mortality advantage** of EGDT over usual care. The results also depend heavily on study population, protocol, implementation, and subgroup characteristics. So, the simple answer is: **EGDT may help some patients, but the evidence does not consistently support a general mortality benefit** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 1) What the enrolled studies found about mortality
The enrolled studies produced a **mixed pattern** of results. In the landmark trial, EGDT reduced in-hospital mortality from 46.5% in the usual-care group to 30.5% in the EGDT group, a **16 percentage-point difference** [N1-F1]. This is the strongest direct evidence in the provided branch reports. However, later studies and meta-analyses did not replicate that benefit so clearly.

A meta-analysis of emergency-department patients with septic shock found **no mortality benefit** overall, with a pooled odds ratio of 1.01 (95% CI 0.88–1.16) and no difference in 90-day mortality from three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. Another meta-analysis also reported no superiority of EGDT for ED patients with septic shock, and a separate meta-analysis found a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.67–1.08) for mortality, with heterogeneity [N3-R5][N3-R4]. A trial-level meta-analysis of individual patient data similarly found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3]. One trial also reported no reduction in 90-day mortality versus usual resuscitation [N2-R2].

So the mortality picture is: **some trials showed benefit, some showed no difference, and the most consistent meta-analyses found no overall mortality advantage** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 2) Which study populations were included and why that matters
The study populations matter a lot because they are not all the same.

- The landmark trial included **adult patients with severe sepsis or septic shock presenting to an emergency department**, with balanced baseline characteristics [N1-F1].
- The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock included **five RCTs** totaling 4735 patients [N3-F2].
- The broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies** as well, which changed the pooled results and increased heterogeneity [N3-F2].
- Another meta-analysis focused specifically on **patients presenting to the ED with septic shock** and reported no mortality benefit from EGDT [N3-R4].

This is important because the setting, disease severity, and timing of intervention can affect outcomes. The landmark trial may have captured a more responsive patient cohort, whereas later trials may have included more heterogeneous or less severely ill patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The branch reports also emphasize that the optimal resuscitation approach remains unclear despite many RCTs, which suggests that the observed differences may reflect real biological variation rather than a single “right” protocol [N4-F3].

## 3) Short-term versus longer-term outcomes
Outcomes span **short-term and longer-term endpoints**.

- The landmark trial reported **in-hospital mortality** as the primary outcome [N1-F1].
- Other studies report **28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality**, with some suggesting benefit but not statistical significance [N2-R1].
- The meta-analyses emphasize **90-day mortality** as the primary outcome [N3-F2].

So the evidence base is not limited to one endpoint. However, the most consistent meta-analysis-level conclusion is that, for ED patients with septic shock, EGDT does **not appear to improve mortality overall** [N3-F2][N3-R5].

## 4) Why results may differ across studies
There are several reasons the results differ across studies.

### a) Differences in EGDT protocol and implementation
EGDT is not implemented in the same way across all studies. The landmark trial used **protocolized early goal-directed therapy before ICU admission**, with predefined interventions and blinded care after randomization [N1-F1]. In contrast, the ProMISe trial used **protocolized 6-hour EGDT versus usual resuscitation**, and the broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies**, which likely had different care settings and intervention components [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity-focused analysis also emphasized that EGDT is a **multicomponent intervention** involving fluids, vasopressors, inotropes, and blood products, and that treatment response varied across patients [N4-F3].

### b) Differences in patient selection and disease severity
Patient selection and baseline disease severity differ across studies. The landmark trial included adults with **severe sepsis or septic shock arriving at the ED**, while later meta-analyses included patients with **septic shock and severe sepsis** and ED patients with **septic shock** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N3-R4]. The branch reports also note that the optimal resuscitation approach remains uncertain, and that the average treatment effect may not reflect individual responses [N4-F3]. This suggests that enrollment criteria, baseline severity, and the stage of disease at presentation can all influence outcomes.

### c) Differences in outcome measurement and follow-up
Outcome measurement and follow-up differ across studies. The landmark trial used **in-hospital mortality** as the primary outcome, while other studies report **28-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality** [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The meta-analyses also included **secondary outcomes** such as organ support and length of stay [N3-F2]. The heterogeneity analysis noted that the “dose” of intervention—such as the amount of fluid or vasopressor—varies across patients, which can complicate comparisons [N4-F3].

These differences help explain why some studies show benefit, others show no difference, and others show harm [N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-F3].

## 5) Trial-level heterogeneity and subgroup differences
Trial-level heterogeneity is central to interpreting the evidence. The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock found **no overall mortality benefit** and **no heterogeneity** in the pooled 90-day mortality estimate from three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. However, including **non-ED trials** increased heterogeneity [N3-F2]. A heterogeneity-focused secondary analysis of two multicenter trials found that **treatment response varied across patients**, with large benefits for some and harm for others [N4-F3]. In that analysis, a machine-learning model predicted individual absolute risk differences, and the validation cohort showed **heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE)**, with treatment response increasing from the lowest to the highest quintiles of predicted risk difference [N4-F3].

- The lowest quintile showed **harm** from EGDT, while the highest quintile suggested **benefit** [N4-F3].
- **Albumin** contributed the most to HTE, suggesting that patient characteristics are a major explanatory factor [N4-F3].
- Individual EGDT components were inconclusive, but the analysis explicitly sought to determine whether patient characteristics or features of intervention delivery could explain HTE [N4-F3].

So the consistent message is: **the effect of EGDT is not uniform; some patients benefit, others do not, and some may be harmed** [N4-F3].

## 6) Limitations and interpretation of the evidence
The evidence has important limitations that affect interpretation.

### a) Study quality and risk of bias
The meta-analysis of ED patients with septic shock reported that the included trials generally scored high for quality except for **lack of blinding** [N3-F2]. The landmark trial did use blinding for clinicians after randomization, which is a strength, but the broader meta-analysis included **non-ED studies**, which may introduce additional heterogeneity [N3-F2]. The heterogeneity analysis also noted that conventional statistical approaches may have been underpowered, which can reduce confidence in subgroup findings [N4-F3].

### b) Sample size and statistical power
The landmark trial had a relatively small sample size: **263 enrolled patients**, with 130 in each group [N1-F1]. By contrast, the meta-analysis included **4735 patients** across five trials and **4063 patients** in three multicenter studies [N3-F2]. Larger studies can detect smaller effects, but the meta-analyses still found no overall mortality benefit, which suggests that the effect, if any, may be small or highly dependent on subgroups [N3-F2].

### c) Dependence on specific subgroups
The results depend heavily on **specific subgroups**. The heterogeneity analysis found that **individual treatment effects varied across patients**, with some harmed and some benefiting, and that albumin was the most important predictor of HTE [N4-F3]. The meta-analysis of individual patient data also found no mortality benefit and higher hospitalization costs [N4-R3]. The broader meta-analysis similarly emphasized heterogeneity in the effect of EGDT across studies [N3-R5]. This means the benefit, if any, is likely concentrated in **particular subgroups** rather than a general population effect [N4-F3][N3-F2].

## 7) Bottom line
Combining the branch reports, the evidence supports the following conclusion:

- **Yes**: there is **one strong landmark trial** suggesting a mortality benefit with EGDT [N1-F1].
- **No overall benefit**: the best meta-analyses and trial-level analyses found **no mortality advantage** of EGDT over usual care for ED patients with septic shock [N3-F2][N3-R5].
- **Mixed results are common**: some studies show benefit, some no difference, and some show harm, especially when subgroups are examined [N2-R1][N4-F3].
- **Heterogeneity matters**: patient characteristics, protocol design, and implementation differences explain why results differ across studies [N4-F3][N3-F2].
- **Interpretation is cautious**: the evidence is limited by study quality, sample size, and subgroup dependence [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## Final judgment
If the question is “does EGDT improve mortality versus usual care?” the most defensible answer, based on the provided evidence, is: **not clearly yes.** The best-supported conclusion is that **EGDT may help some patients, but the evidence does not consistently support a broad mortality benefit** [N1-F1][N3-F2][N4-F3].
